items.title: Scientists gave worms magnetic bacteria. They lived 43% longer

items.title: “We found something never seen before” – A dead star is producing a shock wave that shouldn’t exist
items.summary: A dead white dwarf with no detectable disk has somehow produced a powerful shock wave that appears to have persisted for at least 1,000 years. Its magnetic field may be partly responsible, but astronomers say an unexplained “mystery engine” may also be at work.

items.title: Ancient meteorites reveal a powerful force that helped build the Solar System
items.summary: Ancient grains inside one of the oldest known meteorites reveal that a surprisingly strong magnetic field existed during the solar system’s first 200,000 years. The discovery suggests magnetism worked alongside gravity to help transform a vast cloud of gas and dust into the sun and planetary disk.

items.title: Tracking the movement of plants
items.summary: The flora of the Alps is changing: Species are moving to higher elevations, new plants are appearing and others are disappearing.

items.title: Age-adjusted suicide rate increased from 2014 to 2017 and then plateaued
items.summary: The age-adjusted suicide rate increased from 2014 to 2017 and then did not change significantly from 2017 through 2024, according to a September data brief published by the National Center for Health Statistics.

items.title: Elastic fantastic: The deadly fluid of pitcher plants
items.summary: In the world of carnivorous plants, Venus flytraps—with their showy, snapping reflexes—have long hogged the limelight. But plants have many creative bug-capture strategies, from slippery waxes to vibrating lids to bizarrely textured fluids.

items.summary: The Beast from the East ravaged much of the U.K. and Europe in February and March 2018, bringing severe storms, snow showers and bitter winds. But as the climate changes, rising average temperatures will affect the severity of extremely cold weather like this.

items.title: Researchers expand touchpoints to enhance literacy promotion
items.summary: Literacy promotion programs, combined with community-based support programs, can affect literacy development in Latino children from birth to 18 months of age, Rutgers researchers have found.

items.title: LA fire smoke triggered surge in airborne toxins: How long did they stay?
items.summary: A new study from UCLA provides insights into how the January 2025 Eaton fire affected air quality downwind, showing how levels of toxic airborne contaminants spiked and then dissipated as the burning died down. The research is published in the journal ACS ES&T Air.

items.summary: Rainfall from Hurricane Helene produced a short-term spike in microplastics at three sites in western North Carolina, with microplastic deposition three to 22 times higher than before the storm.

items.title: New research examines CIA failures, Saudi links and missed opportunities before September 11 attacks
items.summary: A new study from the University of Bath sheds light on critical U.S. intelligence failures ahead of the 9/11 attacks, including evidence that changes how the CIA's repeated failure to share information with the FBI about two hijackers should be understood.

items.summary: Curtin University scientists have uncovered an important missing piece in the puzzle of how some coral reefs can recover from climate events, providing information that could help guide future conservation and restoration efforts.

items.summary: A South Korean research team has developed an environmentally friendly ammonia synthesis process that reduces carbon emissions using a membrane that selectively transports hydrogen.

items.title: New findings explain how cells assemble machinery to repair damaged DNA
items.summary: A cell's ability to repair its damaged DNA is one of the most fundamental processes in biology, helping protect us from diseases like cancer. Over the years, researchers have unraveled many of the mechanisms cells use to repair DNA, ultimately leading to precision cancer treatments.

items.summary: As climate change brings more extreme weather events, strengthening families before disasters strike can help protect children's health and well-being, says Mary McKay, a professor at the Brown School at Washington University in St. Louis and an expert on child mental health.

items.summary: Mistletoe is best known from winter traditions as a symbol of luck and affection. For trees, however, the hemiparasitic plant can be a burden: It draws water and nutrients from its hosts. Now the plant could provide a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based industrial adhesives.

items.summary: As a star nears the end of its life, it faces two very different fates: It can explode as a supernova, leaving behind a neutron star, or collapse and become a black hole. What determines the outcome remains one of astrophysics' great unanswered questions.

items.summary: A new survey from the University of Exeter and the University of Surrey reveals broad public support for policies to protect and restore nature in the U.K. Researchers surveyed almost 3,000 people across the country, exploring their feelings, concerns, opinions and experiences in nature.

items.title: Nine lives and counting: Feline aging study marks nine years with new clinical trial
items.summary: The University of Liverpool's Cat Prospective Aging and Welfare Study (CatPAWS), which follows a group of pet cats from middle age into later life, is celebrating more than nine years of work to improve the health and welfare of cats more than 7 years old.

items.title: Frog's coat of bacterial armor helps protect it from fungal disease
items.summary: The bacteria living on frogs' skin could play a vital role in protecting the animals from a deadly fungal disease. A team of researchers led by Penn State scientists found that frogs' natural skin bacteria can help them fight disease and improve their chances of survival.

items.title: Distant time crystals can somehow fall into the same rhythm
items.summary: Researchers have shown that multiple time crystals inside a semiconductor can synchronize their oscillations, much like pendulum clocks gradually falling into the same rhythm. The coupling is carried by spin-polarized electrons, allowing time crystals separated by up to 40 micrometers to lock to a c

items.title: New research: Snack names influence how filling we imagine they will be
items.summary: Imagine being hungry in a grocery store and looking for a snack. You have a choice between Gobo granola bars or Kipi granola bars. Which do you reach for to fill you up? If you're like the participants in our new study, you probably said Gobo.

items.title: Faint young stars reveal spiral galaxy Messier 74 may be twice as large as thought
items.summary: Astronomers have discovered a faint population of young stars extending far beyond the known edge of the nearby spiral galaxy Messier 74. The finding suggests the galaxy is nearly twice as large as previously measured. The new study was published Sept. 4 in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

items.title: Scientists thought they knew how this 70-year-old leukemia drug worked
items.summary: A 70-year-old leukemia drug is still revealing new secrets. Researchers found that removing a protein called NUDT5 protected cells from the drug, even though simply blocking the protein had little effect. The unexpected result points to a hidden cellular role that could help explain why people respo

items.title: Earth's tides are shaped by more than the Moon—and they're changing as the planet warms
items.summary: In some parts of the world, the sea barely rises and falls with the tides. In others, the difference between high and low tide is dramatic. Along Western Australia's Kimberley coast, for example, it can exceed 10 meters (33 feet)—roughly the height of a three-story building.

items.title: Aging muscles may be losing strength for a reason scientists missed
items.summary: A newly identified breakdown in communication between nerves and muscles could help explain why people lose strength as they age. Researchers were able to improve muscle strength in an animal model by targeting a key protein, raising hopes that some age-related weakness could eventually be treated.

items.title: The space race should not endanger Australian wildlife
items.summary: The race to space continues, with the number of rockets launched increasing every year.

items.title: Hungary detects invasive spotted lanternfly for the first time in the EU
items.summary: An invasive insect linked to major agricultural losses in the U.S. has been detected in the European Union for the first time, Hungary's food safety agency said Thursday.

items.title: Researchers build microscopic DNA 'sails' to pull molecules apart
items.summary: Across every cell in the body, molecules are constantly pulling, gripping and releasing under mechanical strain. That force often decides whether a drug sticks to its target, whether a cell holds its shape or whether a disease takes hold.

items.title: Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
items.summary: Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.

items.title: Climate change: Laws and policies must change to prevent future statelessness
items.summary: Australia and other nations should amend laws and practices to address the needs of millions of people expected to move because of climate-related hazards, according to a new report by the Peter McMullin Centre on Statelessness and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

items.title: Q&A: Why should colleges promote student physical activity?
items.summary: Every fall in the United States, millions of young people move to college campuses, away from home for the first time. During this transition, they typically develop new social networks and routines as they learn to live on their own. One of the most important routines college students can intention

items.title: “We just need to go back” – Uranus’ moon Ariel may have hidden a 100-mile-deep ocean
items.summary: Ariel, one of Uranus’ moons, may once have contained a subsurface ocean more than 100 miles deep beneath its fractured icy shell. The finding, combined with similar evidence from Miranda, suggests the distant Uranian system could harbor multiple hidden ocean worlds.

items.title: 1 in 3 Tucsonans exposed to historic water contamination still report signs of psychological trauma
items.summary: Residents of Tucson's south side might remember drinking from the garden hose and bathing their children in tap water. For years, that water was contaminated with industrial solvents that had leaked into the groundwater their wells drew from.

items.title: These massive stars could explain Webb’s strangest galaxies
items.summary: Hubble observations of massive stars in metal-poor dwarf galaxies are revealing clues to why the early universe looks so unusual. Researchers found that stellar winds weaken sharply at extremely low metallicities, potentially allowing massive stars to retain more material and evolve in unexpected wa

items.title: How calcium channels in muscle cells open together
items.summary: Every step we take begins with a burst of calcium inside our muscle cells, causing them to contract. To prepare for action, the cells keep calcium locked in an internal compartment, the sarcoplasmic reticulum. items.title: JWST finds early galaxies were already seeding the universe with heavy elements
items.summary: When the universe was still in its infancy—only 500 million years after the Big Bang, or about 3% of its current age—some of the universe's earliest stars and galaxies had already formed. Astronomers have long predicted that much of the gas surrounding these young galaxies must have remained re

items.title: Bay Area wastewater plants could nearly halve nitrogen cleanup costs by coordinating upgrades
items.summary: Treating polluted water flowing into San Francisco Bay to meet regulatory requirements is going to cost ratepayers money. Exactly how much depends, in large part, on whether the region's wastewater treatment plant operators are willing and able to coordinate infrastructure construction and oper

items.title: Anthropic touts AI-led biology discovery
items.summary: U.S. artificial intelligence startup Anthropic on Wednesday unveiled the first discovery from its molecular biology lab, a previously unknown enzyme system spotted by its Claude model and touted by the company as proof that AI can speed up basic research.

items.title: Archaeological 'breakthrough' could confirm origins of Paris
items.summary: An ancient wall discovered in central Paris was hailed as a "major breakthrough" on Wednesday, as the archaeological find may have settled a long-standing debate about the location of the city's original settlement.

items.title: ADHD and autism diagnoses have surged. A massive study may help explain why
items.summary: A large Danish study found that children diagnosed with ADHD or autism today more closely resemble their peers in the general population than those diagnosed 10 years ago. The shift suggests that rising diagnosis rates may partly reflect broader identification and changing diagnostic patterns, rathe

items.title: AI div objavio prvo veliko otkriće svog laboratorija za molekularnu biologiju
items.summary: AMERIČKA tvrtka za razvoj umjetne inteligencije Anthropic objavila je prvo veliko otkriće svojeg laboratorija za molekularnu biologiju.
